We'll look at Edypus and Homer, the Iliad. They talk about this all the time: fate is something you cannot control; it happens to you, so live life to your best ability. The difference lies in their concept of udeimmonia—living each day to the best of your ability, seizing the day, to win favor from the gods. This is what we call flourishing. 

And that’s why the ancients, particularly the Greeks like Plato and Homer, were superior to us today. They valued ulmonia (flourishing) over mere pleasure. Instead of striving for creative excellence, many today just focus on enjoying life or avoiding sadness.

In the first system, despite the lack of control, it inspires living your best life. In the second system, with complete control, it enslaves us.

Now let's move to the third example. Over this semester, I'll provide evidence that these ideas are true. Today, we're setting up the structure and framework.

Why do we have school? To learn and teach, to get a degree, to graduate, and to gain knowledge.

The correct answer is brainwashing. Everything else is a lie. In school, you attend classes, listen to lectures, read books, take tests, write papers, and receive grades.

Throughout most of human history, learning meant gaining experience. To become a doctor, you'd work in a hospital for 10 years under mentorship. At age 30, the first doctor would be better because the second, who went to Harvard, never worked in a hospital.

In the first system, anyone can be a good doctor; everyone is born with the capacity to learn. In contrast, our current system labels students as smart or stupid, leading them to different paths.

This was not true for most of human history but is today.
